opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Data access is honestly one of the biggest bottlenecks in my work, and it's something I've had to think about from the very beginning of every project.

In medical imaging especially, the data are incredibly sensitive. You're dealing with patient scans, clinical outcomes, pathology reports, and all of that is protected for very good reasons. So the first part of my approach is building relationships. I've found that the most productive work happens when I'm embedded with clinicians: radiologists, surgeons, oncologists, who have a real clinical question they want answered. When the data request comes out of a shared problem rather than a computer scientist showing up and saying "give me your images," the institutional doors open a lot more easily, and the data you get is better annotated and better understood.

The second part is being realistic about the size of the datasets. People hear "AI" and think you need millions of examples, but in many clinical settings, particularly rarer cancers like pancreatic or liver cancers, you might have a few hundred patients at a single institution if you're lucky. So a lot of my methodological work is about squeezing more information out of limited data: using quantitative imaging features, radiomics, incorporating domain knowledge, transfer learning, and being careful about validation so we don't fool ourselves with overfitting.

The third piece is collaboration across institutions. No one hospital has enough data, and models trained at one site often don't generalize to another because of differences in scanners, protocols and patient populations. So I'm a big proponent of multi-site efforts, and increasingly of approaches like federated learning, where the model travels to the data rather than the data leaving the hospital. That respects privacy and governance while still letting us build models that are robust across settings.

And finally, I think we have a responsibility to advocate for better data infrastructure, things like standardized imaging protocols, linked clinical outcomes, and sensible data-sharing agreements. Places with strong, centralized health systems have a real opportunity here. If we get the governance and the trust right, we can unlock data that ultimately benefits the very patients it came from.

r001.rationale: The response supports multi-site collaboration and federated learning, but does not present publicly releasing research data as a way for other teams to use it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Data access is honestly the thing that keeps me up at night more than any algorithmic problem does. In medical imaging, the bottleneck is rarely the model. It's getting enough well-annotated, representative data to train and validate on, and doing that in a way that respects patient privacy and institutional governance.

So my approach has a few parts. First, I spend a lot of time building relationships with clinicians and the institutions themselves, because the data doesn't move without trust. Radiologists, surgeons, pathologists are the people who understand what the images mean and what question is actually worth asking. If you come in as a computer scientist saying "give me your data," you get nowhere. If you come in asking what problem they wish they could solve, you get collaborators, and the data follows.

Second, I think a lot about federated and privacy-preserving approaches, where the model travels to the data instead of the data traveling to us. That lets us work across multiple sites, which matters because a model trained on one hospital's scanners and one hospital's population will often fall apart somewhere else. Generalizability is a data-access problem as much as a modeling problem.

Third, we lean hard on making our work reproducible and, where we can, sharing data and code publicly. The field has been held back by everybody training on their own private silo and reporting numbers nobody can verify. Public benchmark datasets and challenges have done more to move imaging research forward than almost anything else, and we try to contribute to that rather than just consume it.

And finally, I've learned to be realistic about timelines. Ethics approval, data-sharing agreements, de-identification, curation, all of that can take longer than the actual science. You build it into the plan from the start, or it eats the project.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they share data publicly and contrasts this with researchers working in private silos; it also points to public benchmark datasets and challenges as advancing imaging research, communicating that public release lets other teams use the research data.

astra-6.text:
I think the first step is to treat data access as part of the research problem from the beginning. You can have an exciting idea for an imaging or analysis technique, but you need to understand what data are available, how they were collected, and whether they can actually help answer your question. That means working closely with clinicians and the people responsible for those data, with privacy and appropriate permissions built into the process.

And access alone isn’t enough. You also need context: what an image represents, how reliable the labels are, and where information might be missing. I’d rather start with a well-understood dataset and a clear clinical question, then work toward testing across broader settings.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding available data and collaborating with clinicians, but does not present publicly releasing research data as enabling other research teams to use it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is collaboration. To develop useful imaging and analysis techniques, you need access to data that reflects the clinical problem, and that means working closely with the people who collect it and understand its limitations. It’s not just a matter of getting more images; you also need the context to interpret them.

Patient privacy has to be part of that process from the beginning. So I’d approach data access as a shared challenge with clinicians and data custodians: establish what we need, how it can be used responsibly, and how we can evaluate whether the resulting technique will actually help.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collaborating with clinicians and custodians to access data responsibly, but does not say to publicly release research data for other teams to use.
